item.title: 3 Iran-backed operatives indicted for alleged role in terror plots
item.description:
Three Iran-backed operatives have been charged with plotting a terrorist attack at a British Royal Air Force base in the United Kingdom where U.S. troops are stationed, the Justice Department announced on Tuesday.
Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi was indicted in May on federal charges of conspiracy to provide material support to Iran-backed terrorist organizations, including Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata'ib Hizballah. He is accused in an eight-count superseding indictment made public Tuesday of attempting to coordinate with two other operatives to attack the British Royal Air Force base in the U.K. in September.
Al-Saadi is currently in federal custody in New York. In Tuesday's filing, the Justice Department alleged that he had plotted the air base attack with Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national, and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, by "passing them coded messages through third parties."
Mohajeri and al-Hassani are not in custody, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.
Federal prosecutors allege that beginning in August, Al-Saadi "directed and paid" associates in the United Kingdom to prepare for and arrange an attack at RAF Fairford, including directing an unnamed individual to conduct surveillance at the air base. Al-Saadi then allegedly later paid multiple unnamed people to organize vans and barrels of fuel, and to research chemical accelerants and buy metal to be used as shrapnel for a potential attack.
The indictment alleges that three individuals would then drive the vans, filled with fuel, to RAF Fairford, where they would explode.
Prosecutors say Al-Saadi told the individuals to mark the vans with custom decals to disguise themselves as a fuel delivery or pool supply business and directed his family members to pass messages to his co-conspirators.

item.title: Rubio says U.S. has "no need" to restart combat operations in Iran
item.description:
What to know about the Iran war today: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday at a G7 meeting in Paris there was "no need for major combat operations" in Iran because the economic pressure campaign was working well.President Trump said Monday the U.S. was keeping the Iran war at "status quo" but warned that American forces were "locked and loaded."In a 60 Minutes interview that aired Sunday, Mr. Trump said he does not currently see "any reason" to escalate the war. However, he defended starting the conflict as "historically" a good decision, despite its economic impact.
New Updates
3:57 PM
U.S. charges 3 alleged Iranian-backed operatives accused of involvement in attempted attack on U.K. airbase
The Justice Department on Tuesday announced charges against three men described as "Iranian operatives" over their alleged role in an alleged terrorist plot at Britain's RAF Fairford airbase.
Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani were charged in relation to the September incident at the base, which has been used by the U.S. military in its operations against Iran.
"To date, the subjects have been allegedly involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks throughout Europe and the United States in support of Kata'ib Hizballah and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, two U.S. designated foreign terrorist organizations," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.
Al-Saadi, 32, is a citizen of Iraq and Iran; Mohajeri, 48, is a citizen of Iran; and Al-Hassani, 35, is a citizen of Iraq, according to the DOJ.

item.title: Jockey Izzy Neale, 22, dies after her horse falls during race
item.description:
Jockey Izzy Neale died on Tuesday, two days after her horse fell during a race in Australia, the Racing NSW state thoroughbred authority said.
The 22-year-old Neale suffered injuries Sunday when her horse Marnoo fell and suffered a fatal leg injury in the homestretch of a 1-mile race at Warren racecourse.
She was unconscious when airlifted to a hospital, and Racing NSW released a statement Tuesday from her family that she had died.
"Izzy rode horses before she could walk. Her love of horses was a lifelong passion that, more recently, had grown into a love of racing," the statement said of Neale, who rode 88 winners in her career.
Izzy Neale gives a thumbs-up after winning at Rosehill Gardens on July 4, 2026, in Sydney, Australia.
Jeremy Ng/Getty Images
"Through organ donation, Izzy will give others the chance of life, bringing some comfort to our family amid this devastating loss."
Rider Diego Montes de Oca was also dislodged from his horse during the race, Racing NSW said in a statement, adding that he suffered a foot injury but was later discharged from the hospital.
Neale had 699 career starts in her career, local media reported.
Her brother Tommy Neale wrote on Facebook that he couldn't "believe what's happened," adding: "You'll always be my lil baby sister, you were my best friend an we always was so close so I dunno how I'm gonna deal with this."
Izzy Neale smiles after winning at Rosehill Gardens on July 4, 2026, in Sydney, Australia.
Jeremy Ng/Getty Images

item.title: France says Iran behind costly grocery store refrigeration hacks
item.description:
French officials believe Iran was behind nationwide cyberattacks on commercial refrigeration units at hundreds of grocery stores in October, the Paris prosecutor's office said Monday, accusing a cyber unit of Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of carrying out the costly hacks. On Tuesday, France's foreign minister said the country "rules nothing out" in its response to what he called "a terrorist organization that has committed an attack of unprecedented scale and aggression against our country."
The Oct. 11 hacking attack struck major supermarket chains, hitting "700 retail locations across France," according to the prosecutor's office, which said the attack caused "significant food spoilage and triggered roughly twenty fires" as the temperatures in refrigeration units shot up.
The attacks on the French grocery store chains were followed weeks later by similar hacks affecting refrigerators and freezers at supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg and Sweden. A separate cyberattack targeted several blood banks in France, but the products and samples were not damaged.
In August, refrigeration outages at six U.S. military bases sparked an ongoing investigation by the Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division, Thomas Hamilton, a public affairs officer for the department, told CBS News. Hamilton told CBS News this week that the division's Cyber Field Office was working with French law enforcement to understand the refrigeration outages in Europe.
There has been no assertion yet by officials in France, the U.S. or the other European nations hit by the hacks that all of the incidents were connected.
In its statement Monday, the Paris public prosecutor's office said its cybercrime division had opened a judicial investigation on charges including "fraudulent interference with an automated data-processing system and causing damage by means dangerous to persons — both committed as part of an organized group."

item.title: Reported Iran threat sees U.S. move planes from second U.K. base
item.description:
The U.S. military moved nine Stratotanker refueling planes from a base in England to facilities in Germany and Spain on Monday, and The Wall Street Journal quoted sources as saying they had been repositioned due to a threat from Iran.
It is unclear whether the threat was imminent or general, the sources told the newspaper.
A U.S. official told CBS News later Tuesday that there were credible threats against bases in the U.K., without specifying who was behind the threats.
CBS News Confirmed found public aircraft tracking data showing 10 KC-135 Stratotankers were moved from Royal Air Force Base Mildenhall, in southeast England to other locations. One landed at Glasgow Prestwick Airport in Scotland, while four went to Spangdahlem Air Base in Germany and one landed at Ramstein Air Base, the headquarters of the U.S. Forces Europe, also in Germany.
Four more Stratotankers left Mildenhall and arrived Monday at Morón Air Base in southern Spain.
A U.S. Air Force KC-135 Stratotanker aircraft takes off from RAF Mildenhall, in England, as part of an exercise on July 14, 2026.
Ben Birchall/Getty
"We take proactive measures to ensure our aircraft, our people, and our installations remain safe and secure," a U.S. official told CBS News on Tuesday, without commenting on specific aircraft movements.
Three U.S. Osprey tiltrotor transport planes also departed RAF Mildenhall and arrived Tuesday at RAF Lakenheath, another base used by the U.S. in England. It is unclear whether all of the movements were linked to the reported threat from Iran.

item.title: No sign of progress as U.S.-Ukraine-Russia talks get underway
item.description:
The United States, Ukraine and Russia held their first round of trilateral talks in about nine months Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, aimed at ending the war that started when Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered the ongoing, full-scale invasion of the neighboring nation.
After the first of two days of talks set to focus on security guarantees — a long-running demand from Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy — it was clear neither side expected an imminent breakthrough, but Zelenskyy called the discussions "constructive and quite substantive."
President Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner said in a post on X ahead of the meetings that he and Special Envoy Steve Witkoff were "working hard to find a negotiated solution that can deliver lasting peace and create the conditions for a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Ukraine within a more stable European security environment."
U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff (3R), UAE Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al-Nahyan (C) and President Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner (3L) attend talks between members of the Ukrainian and Russian delegations in Abu Dhabi, Nov. 10, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
Altaf Qadri/POOL/AFP/Getty
Kushner indicated this round of talks in the United Arab Emirates capital was just an initial step, but one he said could "build momentum" toward future negotiations. He also suggested a future agreement would involve a security arrangement involving European countries and Russia.
But Russia and Ukraine seemed to pour cold water on the initiative after Tuesday's round of talks.

item.title: Meghan and Harry do first public event since her father's arrest
item.description:
London — Prince Harry and Meghan held hands tightly Tuesday as they stepped into public view for the first time since the Duchess of Sussex's estranged father was arrested in the United States. The FBI detained Thomas Markle Sr., 82, in Florida on Friday after federal prosecutors charged him the previous day with possession of images of child sexual abuse.
Harry and Meghan arrived Tuesday at the European Parliament in Brussels for an event focused on online child safety. Harry and Meghan had been slated to deliver a keynote speech together at the Lost Screen Memorial, but Meghan withdrew, leaving Harry to address the event solo.
Children "deserve to feel safe wherever they are," Harry said, standing alone at the podium, "in a classroom. On a playground. At any time, no matter where they are."
Prince Harry and Meghan, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, arrive at the European Parliament on Nov. 10, 2026, in Brussels, Belgium.
Omar Havana/Getty
The scheduled event's focus was on addressing the perils of online abuse and exploitation of children, but Harry's remarks carried deeper significance for his wife and all those in attendance given the timing.
"I know from people close to her that she is very, very emotional, and that is the reason why she pulled out of giving the speech along with Harry today in Brussels," said Roya Nikkhah, royal editor of Britain's Sunday Times newspaper and a CBS News contributor. "It's been a very difficult time for her."
Nikkhah said Meghan had decided to still attend the event in "solidarity," which she called "a strong indication of how strongly and passionately she feels" about the subject matter.

item.title: Congo court sentences 66 soldiers to death for cowardice, mutiny
item.description:
A military court in the Democratic Republic of Congo has sentenced 66 soldiers to death for cowardice, refusing to obey orders, mutiny and squandering of munition, according to local media reports. The troops spent 12 days on trial at a military court in the town of Walikale, in Congo's eastern North Kivu province, according to Radio Okapi, along with four others who were acquitted and one who was given a 10-year jail sentence.
Military authorities said the aim of the trial was to boost discipline in the armed forces, according to multiple reports by Congolese and international news outlets.
Troops from Congo have been fighting armed groups in the country's resource-rich east for decades, including the M23 group, and the umbrella rebel coalition Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN).
A soldier holds a weapon as soldiers of the Democratic Republic of Congo Army attend a trial in Lubero, July 6, 2024.
SEROS MUYISA/AFP/Getty
The soldiers were arrested on Oct. 20 after being accused of fleeing fighting with FRN fighters, according to CBS News' partner network BBC News.
The country's armed forces have been plagued by accusations of ill-discipline, while soldiers have decried poor pay and equipment, according to the BBC.
In early October, 27 other Congolese government soldiers were sentenced to death for cowardice, Radio Okapi reported.
Congolese authorities reintroduced the death penalty in March 2024 to fight "treason" within the armed forces, according to Amnesty International, which, at the time, said the country's justice system was "plagued by numerous problems, and trials rarely meet fair trial standards as documented."

item.title: U.S. becoming first nation to refuse U.N. Human Rights Council review
item.description:
Geneva — The United States is set on Tuesday to become the first country to fully shun a regular review of its human rights record at the U.N.'s top rights body since it was created two decades ago.
The Trump administration last year pulled the U.S. out of the Human Rights Council, accusing it of an anti-U.S. and anti-Israel bias, and alleging that it didn't uphold the very values it promotes.
Supporters back the council's mandate to keep tabs on human rights in all U.N. member states including the U.S., which has drawn criticism for its policies including strong-arm deportations and targeted killings of alleged drug-runners in the Caribbean and Pacific — which the administration has said are designed to protect U.S. workers and help keep the country safe.
The Geneva-based council regularly examines the rights records of all 193 U.N. member states — generally about every four to five years — as part of a process known as the universal periodic review.
The United States, under President Trump, already skipped its appointment for its review a year ago. The scheduled November 2025 review was pushed back until Tuesday in hopes that the U.S. government might change its mind.
It did not.
"(W)e give no credibility to the agency," a State Department spokesperson said in an email to The Associated Press.
"This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own 'values' as it pushes anti-American rhetoric," the spokesperson said, alleging the council has a "persistent failure to condemn the most egregious human rights violators."
The council says the process requires participation of the country in question, and in the case of an absence of any national representatives, the review cannot go forward.

item.title: Nvidia shares drop amid CEO's alleged Chinese spy affair
item.description: Shares of Nvidia, the world's top AI chipmaker, fell more than 4% on Monday, wiping out about $200 billion in stock market value. The company's CEO admitted to an affair with a woman identified by U.S. intelligence as a former data center executive suspected of spying for China. Jo Ling Kent reports.
